```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(DesignComplexSurvival)
```

This article describes the choices of `ms_looks()` and `ms_test()`: when the
analyses take place, how the efficacy and futility bounds are obtained, and
which approximation of the distribution of the log-rank statistics is used.
The scenario is the delayed treatment effect of the introductory article:
the control group has exponential survival with a median of 12 months, the
hazard ratio is 1 for 6 months and 0.65 afterwards, and 700 patients are
enrolled at 10 per month for 3 months and at 30 per month afterwards.

```{r scenario}
lam <- log(2) / 12
scn <- ms_scenario(ms_model(death = lam, dropout = 0.003),
                   ms_model(time = c(0, 6), death = c(lam, 0.65 * lam), dropout = 0.003),
                   accrual = ms_accrual(time = c(0, 3), rate = c(10, 30)))
cols <- c("time", "events", "info_frac", "z_upper", "hr_upper", "cum_power")
```

## Timing of the analyses

Event-driven analyses take place when the expected number of events reaches
given fractions of the final number. Here the final analysis is at 420
deaths with interim analyses at 50 and 75 percent:

```{r looks-events}
lk <- ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.5, 0.75, 1))
pw <- ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = lk, test = ms_test(), events = 420)
pw$looks[, cols]
```

The final analysis takes place at month `r round(pw$study_duration, 1)`
and the power is `r round(pw$power, 3)`. Analyses can also take place at
calendar times; the numbers of events then follow from the scenario:

```{r looks-calendar}
pw_cal <- ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = ms_looks("calendar", time = c(24, 30, 40)),
                   test = ms_test())
pw_cal$looks[, cols]
```

At the calendar times 24, 30 and 40 months, `r round(pw_cal$looks$events[1])`,
`r round(pw_cal$looks$events[2])` and `r round(pw_cal$looks$events[3])`
deaths are expected and the power is `r round(pw_cal$power, 3)`. The final
analysis can also be placed at a given time after the end of accrual with
`followup` in `ms_power()`, and the looks can mix triggers, for example an
interim analysis at a calendar time and a final analysis driven by events
(see `?ms_looks`).

## Spending functions and efficacy bounds

The efficacy bounds come from alpha spending (Lan and DeMets 1983) with the
event fractions as the spending time. `gs_spend()` gives the cumulative
alpha and `gs_bounds()` the bounds:

```{r spending}
t3 <- c(1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1)
spent <- rbind(OF = gs_spend(t3, type = "OF"),
               Pocock = gs_spend(t3, type = "Pocock"),
               HSD_minus4 = gs_spend(t3, type = "HSD", param = -4))
round(spent, 5)
bounds <- rbind(OF = gs_bounds(t3)$upper,
                Pocock = gs_bounds(t3, sf_eff = "Pocock")$upper,
                HSD_minus4 = gs_bounds(t3, sf_eff = "HSD", param_eff = -4)$upper)
round(bounds, 3)
```

With `spending_time = "information"` in `ms_test()`, the spending time is the
information fraction under the design scenario. With the delayed effect the
two fractions differ at the interim analyses:

```{r spending-time}
pw_info <- ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = lk,
                    test = ms_test(spending_time = "information"), events = 420)
rbind(event_fraction = pw$looks$z_upper, information_fraction = pw_info$looks$z_upper)
```

## Futility bounds

Futility bounds can be fixed, on the Z scale or on the hazard ratio scale,
or obtained by beta spending under the design scenario. With
`binding = FALSE` (the default) the efficacy bounds ignore the futility
bounds, and the type I error is given with and without them:

```{r futility}
tests <- list(
  fixed_hr = ms_test(futility = "fixed", fut_bound = c(1, 1), fut_scale = "hr",
                     binding = TRUE),
  beta_nonbinding = ms_test(futility = "beta", sf_fut = "HSD", param_fut = -2),
  beta_binding = ms_test(futility = "beta", sf_fut = "HSD", param_fut = -2,
                         binding = TRUE))
fut <- lapply(tests, function(te) ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = lk, test = te,
                                           events = 420))
t(sapply(fut, function(x) c(power = x$power, x$type1)))
fut$beta_nonbinding$looks[, c("time", "z_upper", "z_lower", "hr_lower", "prob_lower")]
```

The fixed bound stops the trial at an interim analysis when the estimated
hazard ratio exceeds 1. Its power is `r round(fut$fixed_hr$power, 3)`, against
`r round(pw$power, 3)` without futility bounds: with a delayed effect, the
early hazard ratio is close to 1 and the trial stops for futility with
probability `r round(sum(fut$fixed_hr$looks$prob_lower), 3)`.

## The covariance of the statistics

The argument `variance` of `ms_test()` (and of `lr_moments()` and `lr_cov()`)
chooses the covariance of the standardized statistics. With `"null"` (the
default) the statistics of one endpoint have unit variances and the
correlations of independent increments (Tsiatis 1981). With
`"alternative"`, the variance and covariance of the score under the
alternative hypothesis (Luo et al. 2019) are used instead. With
`"studentized"`, the covariance is the asymptotic covariance of the
statistic that is computed in practice, standardized by the estimated
variance and, for event-driven analyses, taken at a random analysis time.

```{r variance}
mo <- lapply(c(alternative = "alternative", studentized = "studentized"),
             function(v) lr_moments(scn, n = 700, calendar_time = pw$looks$time,
                                    variance = v))
sapply(mo, function(m) m$z_var)
pv <- sapply(c("null", "alternative", "studentized"), function(v)
  ms_power(scn, n = 700, looks = lk, test = ms_test(variance = v), events = 420)$power)
pv
```

The variances of the statistic differ from 1 by at most
`r signif(max(abs(mo$alternative$z_var - 1)), 2)` with `"alternative"` and
`r signif(max(abs(mo$studentized$z_var - 1)), 2)` with `"studentized"`, and
the power is `r round(pv[["null"]], 4)`, `r round(pv[["alternative"]], 4)`
and `r round(pv[["studentized"]], 4)`. The choice affects the power, the
futility bounds by beta spending and, with two endpoints, the familywise
error rate under a partial null hypothesis, but not the efficacy bounds or
the non-binding type I error. In the simulations of `inst/validation/` with
PFS and OS tested together, `"studentized"` agreed best with the simulated
standard deviations and correlations of the statistics (see
`vignette("validation")`).

## Limits of the normal approximation

The power and the type I error rest on the normal approximation of the
log-rank statistics. With unequal allocation and few events the statistic is
skewed. In a design with 2:1 allocation (100 control and 200 treatment
patients), looks at 75 and 150 deaths and O'Brien-Fleming bounds, the
package gives the type I error

```{r skew-package}
ctl_b <- ms_model(time = c(0, 6), death = c(0.05, 0.04), dropout = 0.01)
scn_b <- ms_scenario(ctl_b, ctl_b, allocation = 2,
                     accrual = ms_accrual(time = c(0, 3), rate = c(10, 30)))
pw_b <- ms_power(scn_b, n = 300, looks = ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.5, 1)),
                 test = ms_test(), events = 150)
pw_b$type1[["nonbinding"]]
```

The patient-level simulations of `inst/validation/python/simulate_type1.py`
(both groups with the control model) give the rejection rates in the
direction of benefit and in the opposite direction:

```{r skew-simulation}
sim <- utils::read.csv(system.file("validation", "results", "sim_python_type1.csv",
                                   package = "DesignComplexSurvival"))
rate <- function(v, q) sim$value[sim$variant == v & sim$quantity == q]
groups <- c("B_1:2" = "100 control, 200 treatment",
            "B_2:1" = "200 control, 100 treatment",
            "B_1:1" = "150 in each group")
tab <- data.frame(groups = unname(groups),
                  trials = sapply(names(groups), function(v) sim$n[sim$variant == v &
                    sim$quantity == "reject_upper_any"]),
                  benefit = sapply(names(groups), rate, q = "reject_upper_any"),
                  opposite = sapply(names(groups), rate, q = "reject_lower_any"),
                  row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 4)
```

When the treatment group is the larger group, the probability of rejecting
in favour of the treatment is `r round(rate("B_1:2", "reject_upper_any"), 4)`
instead of `r round(pw_b$type1[["nonbinding"]], 3)`; it falls below the
nominal level when the control group is the larger group, and the deviation
disappears with equal allocation. This is a property of the log-rank test
with few events, not of the computations of the package.

## References

Lan KKG, DeMets DL (1983). Discrete sequential boundaries for clinical
trials. Biometrika 70:659-663.

Luo X, Mao X, Chen X, Qiu J, Bai S, Quan H (2019). Design and monitoring of
survival trials in complex scenarios. Statistics in Medicine 38:192-209.

Tsiatis AA (1981). The asymptotic joint distribution of the efficient
scores test for the proportional hazards model calculated over time.
Biometrika 68:311-315.
